questions.title: What a Function Modifier Actually Does
questions.prompt: In Solidity, what is a function modifier mechanically, how does `onlyOwner` actually enforce access control, and what does the underscore `_;` inside a modifier's body mean?
questions.modelAnswer: A modifier is reusable code that wraps around a function's execution, inserted by the compiler at the point the modifier's name is attached to a function declaration. A typical `onlyOwner` modifier contains a `require(msg.sender == owner, "Not owner")` check followed by the underscore `_;`, and the underscore is the literal marker for 'now run the function body this modifier is attached to.' So when a function declared `function withdraw() public onlyOwner { ... }` is called, execution actually enters the modifier first, evaluates the require statement, and only reaches the function's own body (at the `_;` position) if that check passes -- if it fails, the require reverts the whole transaction before the function body ever runs, refunding unused gas. Modifiers are not a separate access-control system bolted on by the EVM; they are ordinary Solidity code the compiler splices in, which is why the underscore matters and why modifier order is literal execution order when multiple modifiers are stacked on one function.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of a modifier as a function-shaped chunk of code I can 'wrap around' other functions instead of pasting the same check everywhere. `onlyOwner` is almost always just `require(msg.sender == owner); _;` -- the require does the actual access-control check, and that underscore is literally where the original function's body gets dropped in by the compiler. So calling a function with `onlyOwner` doesn't magically restrict access at some EVM level -- it compiles down to 'run this require first, and if it passes, then run what you actually wrote.' That's also why if you stack two modifiers on one function, they run left to right, each one's `_;` handing off to the next, with the real function body only running once all of them have passed their checks. It's a convention for avoiding repeated require statements, not a separate privileged mechanism.
commonMistakes: Describing a modifier as an EVM-level security feature rather than ordinary Solidity code the compiler inlines
Forgetting what the underscore `_;` actually marks -- the insertion point for the wrapped function's body
Not realizing a failed require inside a modifier reverts before the function body ever executes
Assuming modifier order on a function doesn't matter when multiple are stacked
keyPoints: A modifier wraps reusable logic (commonly a require check) around a function's execution
`_;` marks the exact point where the wrapped function's own body is spliced in
A failing require inside the modifier reverts the transaction before the function body runs
Stacked modifiers execute in the order they're listed, left to right

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a modifier compiles down to
Correctly explains the role of the underscore `_;`
Correctly explains onlyOwner's require-based enforcement
Mentions stacked-modifier execution order

questions.title: Mappings vs. Arrays: When Each Actually Fits
questions.prompt: Solidity's `mapping` type looks like a hash table, but it behaves very differently from one under the hood. What can't you do with a mapping that you can do with an array, and why would you choose a mapping over an array for something like token balances?
questions.modelAnswer: A Solidity mapping is implemented as a keccak256-hash-based storage slot lookup: every possible key technically 'exists' already, defaulting to the value type's zero value (0 for uint, false for bool, the zero address for address), and there is no length, no way to iterate over its keys, and no way to ask 'what keys have been set.' An array, by contrast, has a real length you can read and loop over, and supports push/pop. Token balances (`mapping(address => uint256) balances`) are a textbook mapping use case precisely because you only ever need direct lookup by a known key (an address) and never need to enumerate 'every address that holds a balance' on-chain -- iterating all possible addresses would be meaningless anyway. If you genuinely need an enumerable list (e.g. 'here are all addresses that have ever interacted with this contract'), you need to maintain a parallel array alongside the mapping yourself, because the mapping alone cannot answer that.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing that trips people up coming from other languages is that a Solidity mapping doesn't have a size and you can't loop over it -- every key you haven't touched still 'exists' and just returns the zero value for that type, so there's no concept of checking whether a key is 'in' the mapping the way you'd check a dictionary elsewhere. An array actually has a length and you can iterate it, push to it, pop from it. For something like `balances[address]`, a mapping is exactly right because the only thing you ever do is look up one specific address's balance -- you never need to ask the contract 'list every holder,' and honestly you wouldn't want to anyway since that's unbounded and would blow your gas budget. If I actually need an enumerable list of addresses, I keep a separate array alongside the mapping and push to it manually when a new address shows up, because the mapping by itself will never give me that.
commonMistakes: Assuming a mapping key can be checked for 'existence' the way a dictionary key can in other languages
Trying to iterate over a mapping's keys directly, which Solidity doesn't support
Not realizing every unset key already returns a zero value rather than reverting or being undefined
Using an array where a mapping would be both simpler and cheaper, or vice versa, without considering whether enumeration is actually needed
keyPoints: Mappings have no length and cannot be iterated; every key already defaults to the zero value
Arrays have a real length and support push/pop/iteration
Token balances fit a mapping because lookups are always by a known key, never by enumeration
An enumerable list requires maintaining a parallel array alongside the mapping manually

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains mappings cannot be iterated and have no length
Correctly explains the zero-value-default behavior of unset keys
Gives a correct, specific reason balances fit a mapping
Mentions the parallel-array pattern for when enumeration is needed

questions.title: Structs for Grouping Related On-Chain Data
questions.prompt: Why would you reach for a `struct` instead of several separate mappings when modeling something like a user profile or a listing on-chain, and what's the tradeoff of nesting a struct inside a mapping versus an array of structs?
questions.modelAnswer: A struct groups related fields (for example `address seller; uint256 price; bool active;` for a listing) into a single named type, which keeps related data conceptually together and makes function signatures and code far more readable than passing or tracking three or four separate mappings keyed by the same id and hoping they stay in sync. `mapping(uint256 => Listing) listings` gives direct lookup by an id, which is the right choice when listings are looked up individually and don't need to be iterated. `Listing[] listings` gives an enumerable, ordered collection you can loop over, at the cost of needing to search or track an index to find a specific listing, and growing the array has its own gas considerations. The real tradeoff is lookup pattern: choose the mapping form when you'll always know the id you want and never need to enumerate everything; choose the array form when enumeration (or insertion order) genuinely matters, accepting that finding a specific entry by anything other than its index requires a loop.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I catch myself writing three parallel mappings all keyed by the same id -- `sellerOf[id]`, `priceOf[id]`, `activeOf[id]` -- that's my signal to group them into a struct instead, both because it's clearer to read and because it's much harder to let them drift out of sync by accident. Once I have a `Listing` struct, the next decision is mapping versus array: `mapping(uint256 => Listing)` is what I use almost by default, because listings are usually looked up by a known id and I don't need to enumerate 'every listing that exists' on-chain. I only reach for `Listing[]` when I actually need to iterate them in order or return 'all of them' to a caller, and even then I'm aware that's going to get expensive as the array grows, since looping anything on-chain costs gas proportional to its length.
commonMistakes: Tracking several parallel mappings keyed by the same id instead of grouping fields into a struct
Choosing an array of structs when the data is always looked up by a known id and never enumerated
Not recognizing that iterating an on-chain array has gas costs that scale with its length
Assuming a mapping of structs can be iterated the same way an array of structs can
keyPoints: A struct groups related fields into one named type, avoiding desynced parallel mappings
mapping(id => Struct) suits direct lookup by a known id, with no enumeration
Struct[] suits cases needing iteration or insertion order, at the cost of gas that scales with length
The right choice depends on whether lookups are always by known id or require enumeration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the benefit of grouping fields into a struct
Correctly contrasts mapping-of-structs vs array-of-structs
Identifies the gas implication of iterating an array
Gives a concrete, correct example scenario

questions.title: What Events Actually Are and Why Contracts Need Them
questions.prompt: A smart contract can't directly push data to a website the way a server can call a webhook. So what does `emit` actually do when a Solidity contract 'fires' an event, and why can't off-chain applications just rely on a function's return value instead?
questions.modelAnswer: An event declaration (`event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);`) defines a log entry format, and `emit Transfer(...)` writes that entry into the transaction's log data as part of the block, not into contract storage -- logs are cheaper than storage writes and are specifically designed to be read by things watching the chain from outside. A function's return value is only visible to whatever called that function directly, in that same transaction; it is never broadcast anywhere and an off-chain application with no relationship to that specific call has no way to see it. Logs, by contrast, are included in every block and indexed by topics (the `indexed` keyword marks up to three parameters as searchable topics), so any off-chain service -- a backend listening via `contract.on()`, or an indexer like The Graph -- can filter and read them without having made the original call itself. That's the actual reason dApps rely on events rather than return values to know what happened on-chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The distinction that matters is that a return value only goes back to whoever directly called the function, in that transaction, and nobody else -- my backend, which almost never is the one calling the contract directly, would never see it. An event is different: `emit` writes a log entry into the block itself, and logs are just sitting there in every block, available to be filtered and read by anything watching the chain, whether that's my own listener calling `contract.on('Transfer', ...)` or a managed indexer like The Graph. Marking a parameter `indexed` is what makes it filterable -- so I can ask a node 'give me every Transfer event where `to` is this specific address' efficiently, instead of scanning every log myself. That's really the whole reason events exist: they're the mechanism a contract has for broadcasting 'something happened' to the outside world, since it has no way to make an outbound HTTP call the way a normal backend would.
commonMistakes: Assuming an off-chain application can read a function's return value without having called it directly
Not knowing that logs/events are cheaper than storage writes and are a separate data channel
Forgetting what the `indexed` keyword does for filtering event queries
Thinking a contract can push data out to a server the way a webhook does
keyPoints: emit writes a log entry into the transaction/block, not into contract storage
Return values are only visible to the direct caller, in that same transaction
Logs are readable by any off-chain listener or indexer watching the chain, without having made the call
indexed parameters (up to 3) make an event's fields efficiently filterable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what emit actually writes and where
Correctly explains why return values don't serve this purpose
Explains how off-chain listeners/indexers actually consume events
Mentions the role of indexed parameters

questions.title: view, pure, and State-Changing Functions
questions.prompt: What do the `view` and `pure` keywords actually promise about a Solidity function, and why does calling a `view` function cost no gas from outside the chain but potentially cost gas if called from inside another contract's transaction?
questions.modelAnswer: `view` promises the function reads contract state but never modifies it; `pure` promises it does neither -- it doesn't even read state, only operates on its inputs. These aren't just documentation; the compiler enforces them, rejecting a `view` function that tries to write storage. The gas-cost nuance is about where the call originates: a 'call' made by an external client (a wallet, a dApp's frontend via RPC) to a `view` function doesn't actually create a transaction at all -- the node just executes it locally against current state and returns the answer, so no gas is spent and nothing is mined. But if that same `view` function is invoked by another contract as part of a state-changing transaction, it still runs as part of the overall transaction's execution and its computation still consumes gas, because the whole transaction it's embedded in is being executed and paid for on-chain regardless of whether this particular function itself changes anything.
questions.professionalAnswer: `view` means 'I read state but I promise not to write it,' `pure` means 'I don't even touch state, I just compute something from my inputs' -- and the compiler actually checks this, so you can't sneak a storage write into a function marked view. The gas question depends entirely on how the call gets made. If my backend or a user's wallet just calls a view function directly over RPC to read something -- say, `balanceOf(address)` -- that's not a transaction at all, it's a local read against the node's current state, so there's no gas and nothing goes into a block. But the moment that same view function gets called from inside another contract's function, as part of an actual transaction someone's paying for, its execution is just more computation inside that transaction, so it adds to the gas cost of that overall transaction even though the view function itself never writes anything.
commonMistakes: Treating view/pure as mere documentation rather than compiler-enforced guarantees
Assuming a view function is always free regardless of how it's invoked
Not distinguishing a direct external RPC call from a call made inside another contract's transaction
Confusing pure (no state access at all) with view (read-only state access)
keyPoints: view functions read but don't write state; pure functions don't touch state at all; both are compiler-enforced
A direct external call to a view function is a local read, not a transaction -- no gas, nothing mined
A view function called inside another contract's transaction still adds to that transaction's gas cost
The gas cost depends on the calling context, not on the view/pure keyword itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines view and pure and that they're compiler-enforced
Correctly explains why direct external view calls cost no gas
Correctly explains why a view call inside a transaction still costs gas
Clear, accurate terminology throughout

questions.title: require, revert, and assert: Picking the Right Error Tool
questions.prompt: Solidity gives you three different ways to abort execution: `require`, `revert`, and `assert`. What's the actual difference in intent and gas behavior between them, and when would you reach for each?
questions.modelAnswer: `require(condition, "message")` is for validating external input and preconditions you expect could legitimately fail -- insufficient balance, caller not authorized, a zero address passed in -- and it refunds remaining gas on failure. `revert("message")` does the same abort-and-refund-remaining-gas behavior but without a leading boolean condition, used when the check logic is more complex than a single expression (e.g. inside an `if/else` branch) or when throwing a custom error type. `assert(condition)` is meant for invariants that should be mathematically impossible to violate if the contract's logic is correct -- it signals an internal bug rather than bad external input, and historically consumed all remaining gas (pre-0.8.0); from Solidity 0.8 onward both require and assert revert with remaining gas refunded, but the semantic distinction still matters: reaching a failed assert means something is actually wrong with the contract's own logic, not that a user did something invalid.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat these as answering different questions. `require` is 'is this input or precondition valid' -- wrong caller, insufficient funds, bad parameter -- and it's the one I reach for by default because it's just a condition plus a clear error message, and the caller gets their unused gas back. `revert` is functionally the same abort behavior, but I use it when the check doesn't fit cleanly into one boolean expression, like deep inside an if/else chain, or when I'm throwing a custom error for cheaper gas and better tooling support. `assert` is the odd one out semantically -- it's meant to say 'this should be literally impossible given correct contract logic,' like an invariant on total supply never going negative. If an assert ever actually fires, that's not the user's fault, that's a bug in my contract, and I want that distinction visible in the code even though, since Solidity 0.8, the gas-refund behavior between require and assert converged.
commonMistakes: Using assert for ordinary input validation that a user could legitimately trigger
Not knowing require and revert produce the same practical abort/refund behavior, differing mainly in syntax/use-case
Assuming assert still consumes all gas on every compiler version (true pre-0.8.0, not after)
Treating the three as interchangeable with no semantic distinction
keyPoints: require validates external input/preconditions and refunds remaining gas on failure
revert provides the same abort behavior for more complex conditional logic or custom errors
assert signals an internal invariant violation -- a bug in the contract's own logic, not bad input
Post-Solidity-0.8.0, require and assert both revert with remaining gas refunded; the semantic distinction remains important

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes require's intended use case
Correctly distinguishes revert's intended use case
Correctly distinguishes assert's intended use (invariants/bugs)
Accurately describes gas-refund behavior and version nuance

questions.title: Contract Immutability, Gas, and the ABI
questions.prompt: Once a smart contract is deployed, its code literally cannot be changed at that address. What does that immutability actually mean in practice for fixing bugs, and separately, what is the ABI and why does an off-chain application need it to call the contract at all?
questions.modelAnswer: Deployed bytecode at a contract address is fixed permanently -- there is no 'edit and redeploy to the same address' operation; fixing a bug means deploying an entirely new contract at a new address (or using a deliberate, more complex upgradeability pattern like a proxy, which is a separate design decision made in advance, not something immutability allows after the fact). This is why audits and testing matter so much more here than in ordinary backend code, where a bug can just be patched and redeployed. The ABI (Application Binary Interface) is a JSON description of the contract's functions, their parameter types, and return types -- it's what a library like ethers.js or viem uses to encode a function call into the raw bytecode format the EVM actually expects, and to decode the raw bytes that come back into a usable return value. Without the ABI, an off-chain application would have no way to know how to format a call to a specific function or interpret its response -- the contract's deployed bytecode alone doesn't expose a human-readable interface.
questions.professionalAnswer: Immutability means exactly what it sounds like -- once that bytecode is at an address, there's no 'patch it' option at all. If there's a bug, the real options are deploy a brand new contract at a new address and migrate everyone over, or have built a proxy/upgradeability pattern in from day one, which is a whole separate architectural decision you have to make before deployment, not something you can retrofit afterward. That's the actual reason testing and audits get taken so seriously here -- there's no quick hotfix the way there is for a web server. The ABI is the piece that makes any of this callable from outside at all: it's a JSON spec of every function's name, its parameter types, and its return types, and tools like ethers.js use it to translate a normal-looking function call in my code into the raw encoded bytes the EVM actually expects, and then decode whatever bytes come back into something usable. The deployed bytecode itself is just opcodes -- the ABI is the map that makes it possible to talk to it meaningfully.
commonMistakes: Assuming a bug can be 'patched' in place at the same contract address
Not distinguishing an unplanned fix (new contract, new address) from a deliberately designed proxy/upgradeability pattern
Thinking the ABI is part of the deployed bytecode rather than a separate off-chain artifact
Not explaining what the ABI is actually used for (encoding calls, decoding responses)
keyPoints: Deployed bytecode at an address is permanently fixed; there's no in-place edit
Fixing a bug means a new contract at a new address, or a pre-planned upgradeability pattern
The ABI is a JSON description of a contract's callable interface (functions, params, return types)
Libraries use the ABI to encode calls into EVM-expected bytes and decode responses back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what immutability means for bug fixes
Correctly distinguishes new-deployment from pre-planned upgradeability
Correctly defines the ABI and its contents
Correctly explains why off-chain tools need the ABI to call the contract

questions.title: Building on OpenZeppelin Instead of Writing ERC-20 From Scratch
questions.prompt: Why do most production ERC-20 and ERC-721 contracts inherit from OpenZeppelin's contracts instead of implementing the token standard by hand, and what does `contract MyToken is ERC20 { ... }` actually do under the hood?
questions.modelAnswer: Writing `contract MyToken is ERC20("MyToken", "MTK") { ... }` uses Solidity's inheritance to pull in OpenZeppelin's full, already-implemented and widely audited ERC-20 logic (transfer, approve, transferFrom, balanceOf, the Transfer and Approval events, correct allowance accounting) as the base contract, and `MyToken` gets all of that functionality automatically without rewriting it. The practical reason production contracts do this rather than hand-rolling the standard is that OpenZeppelin's implementations have been reviewed by thousands of auditors and used across enormous amounts of deployed value, so subtle bugs in allowance accounting or edge cases (zero-address transfers, overflow) have already been found and fixed, whereas a hand-written version starts from zero of that scrutiny. `MyToken` then typically only needs to add its own specific behavior on top -- a constructor that mints an initial supply, or overriding a specific hook -- rather than reimplementing the whole standard.
questions.professionalAnswer: Inheriting from OpenZeppelin's ERC20 means my contract's declaration literally says 'I am an ERC20, plus whatever extra I add,' and the compiler pulls in their already-written transfer, approve, transferFrom, balanceOf, and the required events, correctly implemented. The reason I'd basically never hand-write ERC-20 logic from scratch for anything real is that OpenZeppelin's version has had enormous scrutiny -- it's been audited repeatedly and used in contracts holding huge amounts of value, so the subtle bugs (allowance underflow, zero-address edge cases, reentrancy in weird token hooks) have already been found by people far more adversarial than I'd be testing my own code. My `MyToken` contract usually just adds a constructor that mints the initial supply to whoever deploys it, or maybe overrides one specific function -- the heavy lifting of 'correctly implement the standard' is inherited, not rewritten.
commonMistakes: Describing inheritance here as copy-pasting code rather than Solidity's actual inheritance mechanism
Not identifying audit history/scrutiny as the real reason to prefer OpenZeppelin over a hand-written implementation
Assuming inheriting ERC20 still requires reimplementing transfer/approve/transferFrom yourself
Not mentioning that the child contract typically only adds specific extra behavior, not the whole standard
keyPoints: `is ERC20` uses Solidity inheritance to pull in OpenZeppelin's already-implemented standard functions and events
OpenZeppelin's implementation benefits from extensive audit history and real-world scrutiny
Hand-writing the standard risks reintroducing already-solved bugs (allowance edge cases, overflow, etc.)
The child contract typically only adds specific extra behavior (minting logic, hooks) on top

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what `is ERC20` does mechanically
Gives the real reason (audit history/scrutiny) for preferring OpenZeppelin
Correctly describes what's inherited vs. what the child typically adds
Clear, accurate terminology

questions.title: Reentrancy, Conceptually: Why the DAO Hack Worked
questions.prompt: At a conceptual level, what is a reentrancy attack, and why did sending Ether to an external address before updating a contract's internal balance create the opening that the original DAO hack exploited?
questions.modelAnswer: A reentrancy attack exploits the fact that sending Ether to an address (or calling an external contract) can hand execution control to that external code before the current function has finished running -- if the receiving address is itself a malicious contract, its fallback/receive function can call straight back into the original contract, re-entering a function that hasn't finished its own bookkeeping yet. The DAO's withdraw function sent Ether to the caller first and only decremented their recorded balance afterward; a malicious contract on the receiving end used its receive function to immediately call withdraw again, and because the balance hadn't been decremented yet, the check against it still passed, letting it withdraw again and again, recursively, before the first call had ever gotten to subtract anything. The vulnerability was purely about ordering: external interaction before state update, not some flaw in Ethereum itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core idea is that handing Ether (or calling) to an external address isn't a dead-end -- if that address is a contract, your transaction has just given it a chance to run its own code and call back into you before you've finished your own function. The DAO's bug was doing `send Ether to caller` and only after that `decrement caller's recorded balance`. A malicious contract receiving that Ether had a receive function that immediately called withdraw again -- and because the balance update hadn't happened yet, the balance check inside that re-entered call still saw the old, unreduced balance and let it through. That one re-entered call itself could re-enter again, recursively, draining funds across many nested calls before the very first call ever got to the line that was supposed to decrement anything. It's entirely an ordering bug -- external call before internal state update -- not a flaw in the EVM or in Solidity itself.
commonMistakes: Describing reentrancy as a flaw in Ethereum/the EVM rather than an ordering bug in the vulnerable contract's own code
Not explaining that sending Ether to a contract address can hand it execution control
Missing that the balance check passed on re-entry specifically because the decrement hadn't happened yet
Describing the attack as a single exploit rather than a recursive/nested chain of re-entered calls
keyPoints: Sending Ether/calling an external address can hand that address (if it's a contract) execution control
The vulnerable pattern: external interaction happens before the internal state update that should prevent repeat withdrawal
A malicious receiving contract's fallback/receive function re-enters the original function before it finishes
The balance check passes on re-entry because the balance hadn't been decremented yet -- a pure ordering bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that external calls can hand over execution control
Correctly identifies the ordering flaw (external call before state update)
Correctly explains how the DAO's specific exploit used this
Clear framing that this is an ordering bug, not an EVM flaw

questions.title: What an RPC Provider Actually Is and Why a Backend Needs One
questions.prompt: A dApp's backend never runs its own full Ethereum node. What is an RPC provider actually doing for it, and what's the real difference between a request like `eth_getBalance` going to Infura/Alchemy versus your backend somehow talking to the blockchain directly?
questions.modelAnswer: A blockchain node is the thing that actually stores (or can reconstruct) chain state and participates in the peer-to-peer network; running one yourself means real infrastructure -- disk space for the chain data, bandwidth, and operational maintenance. An RPC provider (Infura, Alchemy, QuickNode, etc.) runs that node infrastructure for you and exposes it over a JSON-RPC HTTP/WebSocket API, so your backend's call to `eth_getBalance` is really just an HTTP request to the provider's endpoint, which the provider's own node answers by actually reading its local copy of chain state. There is no way to 'talk to the blockchain directly' without going through some node -- what a backend developer actually chooses between is running their own node (full control, full operational burden) or using a managed RPC provider (someone else runs and maintains the node, you just make API calls to it, typically for free up to a rate limit and then paid tiers beyond that).
questions.professionalAnswer: There's no version of this where my backend talks to 'the blockchain' as some abstract thing -- it always talks to a specific node, full stop. The question is just whose node. Running my own means real infrastructure: syncing and storing the chain, keeping it online, keeping it patched. Using Infura or Alchemy means they've already done all of that, and I just send a JSON-RPC call like `eth_getBalance` to their HTTP endpoint and they answer it from their node's own copy of the chain state. For almost any backend I'm building, especially early on, a managed provider is the obvious default -- free tier is usually enough to start, and I'm not signing up to operate blockchain infrastructure as a side effect of building an app. The only reasons I'd run my own node are things like needing guaranteed uptime independent of a vendor, extremely high request volume where a vendor's pricing stops making sense, or specific data access patterns a managed provider's API doesn't expose well.
commonMistakes: Implying there's a way to query the blockchain without any node being involved
Not knowing RPC calls are literally JSON-RPC requests over HTTP/WebSocket to a specific endpoint
Overstating what 'running your own node' requires, or underestimating it
Not giving a concrete reason someone would run their own node instead of using a managed provider
keyPoints: All chain access goes through some node; there's no way to bypass that
An RPC provider runs node infrastructure and exposes it as a JSON-RPC API over HTTP/WebSocket
eth_getBalance and similar calls are literal JSON-RPC requests answered from the provider's node state
The real choice is self-hosted node (control, operational burden) vs. managed provider (convenience, rate limits/cost)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that all chain access goes through a node
Correctly explains what an RPC provider exposes and how
Correctly frames the real self-hosted vs. managed-provider tradeoff
Clear, accurate terminology

questions.title: Polling vs. WebSocket Subscriptions for On-Chain Events
questions.prompt: A backend needs to know as soon as a specific contract emits an event. What's the actual mechanical difference between polling for new events and subscribing over a WebSocket, and why would you pick one over the other?
questions.modelAnswer: Polling means your backend repeatedly calls something like `eth_getLogs` on a schedule (every N seconds), asking the node 'give me any matching logs since the last block I checked,' and the backend has to track its own 'last processed block' cursor between calls -- it's a pull model, and the real-world detection latency is bounded by the polling interval. A WebSocket subscription (`eth_subscribe` with a 'logs' filter) opens a persistent connection, and the node pushes new matching logs to the backend as they occur, with latency bounded only by block time and network delay -- it's a push model. Polling is simpler to reason about, survives connection drops more gracefully (you just resume from your last known block), and works with any provider; WebSocket subscriptions give lower latency but require handling reconnects and resubscription carefully, since a dropped connection silently stops delivering events until you notice and reconnect.
questions.professionalAnswer: Polling is the pull model -- my service wakes up every so often, asks the node for logs matching my filter since the last block I actually processed, and I'm the one keeping track of where I left off. WebSocket subscriptions flip that: I open a persistent connection and tell the node 'push me anything matching this filter,' and it does, as events happen, without me asking again. The real tradeoff is latency versus resilience. Polling has latency bounded by however often I poll, but it's dead simple to recover from a crash or dropped connection -- I just pick up from the last block number I have stored. WebSockets get me near-real-time notification, but if that connection drops silently, I stop getting events and don't necessarily know it until I notice something's missing, so I need explicit reconnect-and-resubscribe logic, and ideally a periodic poll as backup, to actually trust it in production.
commonMistakes: Describing polling or WebSocket subscriptions without mentioning which side is tracking state (the pull/push distinction)
Assuming a WebSocket subscription can't silently drop without the backend noticing
Not mentioning that polling requires the backend to track its own last-processed-block cursor
Treating one approach as strictly better rather than a latency/resilience tradeoff
keyPoints: Polling is a pull model: the backend repeatedly asks for logs since its own tracked last block
WebSocket subscriptions are a push model: the node sends matching logs as they occur
Polling has higher, interval-bounded latency but recovers simply from drops
WebSocket subscriptions give lower latency but need explicit reconnect/resubscribe handling for dropped connections

questions.title: The Oracle Problem, Explained Plainly
questions.prompt: Smart contracts can only natively see data that's already on their own blockchain. What exactly is 'the oracle problem,' and why can't a contract just make an HTTP request to fetch something like a real-world price?
questions.modelAnswer: The EVM executes deterministically -- every node in the network re-executes every transaction and must arrive at the exact same result, which is only possible if execution depends solely on data already in the blockchain's own state. An HTTP request is fundamentally non-deterministic from the chain's point of view: it could return different data to different nodes, time out for some and not others, or change between the time one node and another node processes the same transaction, which would break the entire consensus model. That's the oracle problem: smart contracts need real-world data (prices, weather, sports scores, randomness) for huge classes of useful applications, but they structurally cannot fetch it themselves. The practical solution (e.g. Chainlink) is a decentralized network of off-chain nodes that fetch external data, reach agreement on it off-chain, and then submit it on-chain as a regular transaction -- at which point it's just deterministic contract state like anything else, and the contract reads it the normal way, without ever making an external call itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: Every node re-executing a transaction has to get the identical result, every time, forever -- that's what makes the chain trustworthy without needing a central authority. An HTTP call breaks that completely, because it could come back differently to different nodes, or at different times, which would mean nodes disagree about what happened and consensus falls apart. So a contract genuinely cannot make an outbound request itself -- it's not a missing feature, it's structurally incompatible with how the chain stays deterministic. The oracle problem is just the name for the resulting gap: a huge number of useful contracts need real-world data, but the chain can't fetch it on its own. The fix, like Chainlink's price feeds, is a decentralized set of nodes that go get the data off-chain, agree on a value among themselves, and then submit that value on-chain as an ordinary transaction -- by the time my contract reads it, it's just regular contract state, deterministic like everything else, because the actual 'fetching' already happened somewhere else entirely.

questions.title: Sign-In With Ethereum: What a Signature Actually Proves
questions.prompt: In a Sign-In With Ethereum (SIWE) flow, a user signs a message with their wallet instead of typing a password. What does that signature actually prove to your backend, and what does it deliberately not prove?
questions.modelAnswer: The backend generates a structured message (including a domain, a nonce, and often a statement and expiration) and the user's wallet signs it with their private key; the backend then verifies that signature against the claimed wallet address using standard ECDSA signature recovery. A valid signature proves, cryptographically, that whoever produced it controls the private key corresponding to that address -- nothing more. It does not prove the address belongs to a specific real-world identity, that the wallet hasn't been compromised, or anything about the account's history or token holdings; those would need to be checked separately if relevant. The nonce in the signed message exists specifically to prevent replay -- without a unique, server-issued nonce tied to this login attempt, a captured valid signature from a previous session could be resubmitted to impersonate the same login again.
questions.professionalAnswer: What a valid signature actually proves, and only this, is that whoever signed that exact message controls the private key behind that address -- it's proof of key possession, full stop. It says nothing about who that person is in the real world, whether their wallet is compromised by malware, or what's actually in that wallet. If my app needs any of that, I'm checking it separately -- the signature itself only answers 'does this request genuinely come from the holder of this address's private key.' The nonce my backend generates and includes in the message to be signed matters a lot here: it has to be unique per login attempt, because without it, someone who captured a previously valid signature (say, by snooping network traffic, or because a frontend logged it somewhere it shouldn't have) could replay that exact same signed message later and get authenticated again, without ever touching the real wallet. The nonce ties the signature to this one specific login attempt and kills that replay path.

Describing SIWE as equivalent to a password rather than cryptographic proof of key possession
Omitting that the backend, not the wallet, is responsible for generating the nonce and verifying the signature

If that's what I find, the uncomfortable truth is there's no in-place fix; the contract is what it is. questions.prompt: You deploy a contract to a testnet successfully, but every call to one specific function reverts with no obvious error message in the frontend. How do you track down why?
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is getting a real error message rather than a generic 'transaction reverted' from the frontend -- calling the function as a static call (or simulating it, e.g. via `eth_call` or a library's `.staticCall`) before actually sending the transaction surfaces the specific revert reason without spending gas. If the revert reason itself isn't informative, the next step is checking the function against the ABI being used by the frontend -- a stale or mismatched ABI (e.g. after redeploying with a changed signature) is a common, completely non-obvious cause of calls reverting with no clear reason. Also worth checking: whether the function has a modifier (onlyOwner, a paused check) that's silently failing because the caller's address or the contract's state isn't what was assumed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I do is stop trying to read the error from the frontend's generic failure message and instead simulate the call directly -- staticCall in ethers, or calling the contract's function as a read against current state -- which actually surfaces the require message that's failing, instead of just 'reverted.' If that message is clear, great, now I know the real cause. If calls are reverting with literally no reason at all, my next suspicion is a stale ABI -- if I redeployed the contract with a changed function signature and the frontend is still using an old ABI, the encoded call data doesn't match what's actually at that address, and that fails in a way that doesn't look like a normal require failure. I'd also double check any modifier on that function -- an onlyOwner or paused check failing silently because the caller isn't who I assumed, or the contract's in a state I didn't expect.

Not checking for a stale/mismatched ABI after a redeployment with a changed function signature
Overlooking a modifier (onlyOwner, paused) as the actual source of the revert
Assuming the contract itself has a bug before ruling out a frontend/integration mismatch

Debugging should start from the contract's real revert reason, not the frontend's generic error

questions.title: Your Event Listener Missed Events During a Chain Reorg
questions.prompt: Your backend's event listener logged a contract event, but a few minutes later a chain reorg happened and that event's transaction is no longer in the canonical chain -- yet your database still reflects it as having happened. How do you both diagnose and prevent this?
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause is treating an event as final the instant it's seen in a new block, when blocks near the tip of the chain can still be reorganized out -- especially on networks with probabilistic finality. Diagnosing it means checking whether the specific transaction hash the event came from is still included in the current canonical chain (a block explorer or `eth_getTransactionReceipt` will show it as null or in a different block if reorged out). Prevention means not treating recent events as final: waiting for a minimum number of confirmations (block depth) before writing the event's effects into application state as settled, and for critical data, periodically re-verifying recently-processed events are still present in the canonical chain, rolling back/correcting application state if one is found to have been reorged out.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake, looking back, is treating 'I saw this event in a block' as the same thing as 'this definitely happened,' when blocks near the current tip can still get reorganized away, especially on networks without instant finality. To diagnose a specific case, I'd check the transaction hash from that event directly -- if `eth_getTransactionReceipt` now returns null or shows it in a different block than before, that confirms it was reorged out. Going forward, the real fix is waiting for a confirmation depth (N blocks) before treating an event as settled in my own database, and for anything that really matters, having a background check that periodically reverifies recently-processed events are still in the canonical chain, so I can detect and correct a reorg after the fact instead of just hoping it doesn't happen.
commonMistakes: Treating an event seen in the latest block as permanently final with no reorg risk
Not checking the transaction's current receipt/inclusion when investigating a suspected reorg
No confirmation-depth buffer before committing an event's effects as settled application state
No process for detecting or correcting already-processed events that get reorged out

Checking the transaction's current receipt confirms whether it's still in the canonical chain
Waiting for a confirmation-depth buffer before treating an event as settled reduces this risk
Periodic reverification can detect and correct already-processed events that got reorged out

questions.title: Your Backend Starts Getting Rate-Limited by Its RPC Provider
questions.prompt: In production, your backend starts intermittently failing chain reads with 429 (rate limit) errors from your RPC provider, right after a traffic spike. How do you diagnose the real cause and fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is checking the provider's dashboard/logs for actual request volume against the plan's rate limit, to confirm this really is a volume problem rather than, say, a burst of retried failed requests making the real load worse. A common root cause is inefficient usage -- making many redundant small RPC calls (e.g. one call per item in a loop, rather than batching) or polling too frequently -- rather than genuinely needing that much throughput. Fixes include batching requests where the provider's API supports it, adding client-side caching for data that doesn't change every block, adding backoff/retry logic instead of immediately retrying on a 429 (which otherwise compounds the problem), and as a structural fix, configuring provider failover across multiple RPC endpoints so one provider's rate limit isn't a single point of failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: First I check the provider's own dashboard to see actual request volume against my plan's limit -- that tells me immediately whether this is genuinely too much legitimate traffic or whether my own retry logic is making things worse by hammering the same failed requests repeatedly. Usually when I dig in, the real issue isn't that I need a bigger plan, it's that something in my code is making way more calls than necessary -- a loop calling the RPC once per item instead of batching, or a poller running far more frequently than the data actually changes. I'd fix the inefficient usage first, add exponential backoff so a 429 doesn't immediately trigger another request, and add caching for anything that doesn't need a fresh on-chain read every single time. Longer term, I'd set up failover across at least two RPC providers, so a rate limit or outage on one doesn't take down chain access for the whole backend.
commonMistakes: Immediately upgrading the provider plan without checking whether usage is actually inefficient
Retrying a rate-limited request immediately without backoff, compounding the problem
Not identifying redundant/uncached calls as the real root cause of excessive request volume
Having no failover across multiple RPC providers, creating a single point of failure

questions.title: A Price-Triggered Service Acted on a Stale Oracle Price
questions.prompt: A backend service that triggers an action when ETH price crosses a threshold (via a Chainlink price feed) fired based on a price that turned out to be several hours old due to a temporary issue upstream. How do you diagnose this happened and prevent it?
questions.modelAnswer: The `latestRoundData()` response includes an `updatedAt` timestamp, and the root cause here is almost certainly that the service read the `answer` field without ever checking `updatedAt` against the current time -- a price feed updates on a heartbeat/deviation schedule, not continuously, and under rare upstream conditions it can go longer than expected between updates. Diagnosing means checking historical round data around the incident to confirm `updatedAt` really was stale at the moment the service acted. Prevention means adding an explicit staleness check -- reject (or alert on) any price whose `updatedAt` is older than some acceptable threshold tied to that feed's expected heartbeat, rather than trusting whatever `latestRoundData()` returns unconditionally.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest root cause here is almost certainly that the service trusted `answer` from latestRoundData without ever looking at `updatedAt`. Every Chainlink feed updates on a heartbeat or deviation threshold, not every single block, and that's normally fine -- but it means 'latest' doesn't guarantee 'recent' under unusual conditions. To confirm, I'd pull the round data from around the time of the incident and check what updatedAt actually was relative to when the action fired. Going forward, I'd add an explicit staleness guard -- if updatedAt is older than, say, the feed's expected heartbeat plus some buffer, treat the price as untrustworthy and don't act on it, alerting instead so a human can look. That one check is the difference between a price feed being a nice convenience and being something I can actually depend on for triggering real actions.

Assuming 'latest' always means 'recent' for an oracle feed
Not investigating historical round data to confirm the actual staleness at the time of the incident
No staleness threshold/guard before acting on a price, versus alerting a human

Price feeds update on a heartbeat/deviation schedule, not continuously
Diagnosing means confirming the actual updatedAt value at the time of the incident
Prevention means an explicit staleness guard before acting on any oracle price

questions.title: Transactions Failing With 'Nonce Too Low' or 'Replacement Underpriced'
questions.prompt: Your backend sends several transactions from the same wallet in quick succession, and some of them fail with 'nonce too low' or 'replacement transaction underpriced.' What's actually going wrong, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Each transaction from a given address must use a nonce exactly one higher than the previous confirmed (or pending) transaction from that same address, in strict sequence; if the backend lets the library auto-fetch the 'next nonce' for each transaction independently and fires several off concurrently before any of them confirm, multiple transactions can end up requesting the same nonce value, causing later ones to fail as 'nonce too low' once an earlier one with that nonce confirms, or 'replacement underpriced' if the node interprets the duplicate-nonce transaction as an attempted (but insufficiently-priced) replacement of the pending one. The fix is managing nonces explicitly and sequentially in the backend: track the next nonce to use as application state, incrementing it locally immediately after each transaction is submitted (not waiting for confirmation), rather than asking the provider for 'the next nonce' fresh before every send.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always a concurrency bug in how nonces get assigned, not anything wrong with the chain. If I let the library ask the node for 'what's the next nonce' separately for each of several transactions I'm firing off close together, and none of them have confirmed yet, I can easily get the same nonce handed out twice, because the node's view of 'next nonce' hasn't moved yet. The real fix is to stop asking per-transaction and instead manage the nonce myself as application state -- fetch it once, then increment my own local counter immediately after each send, not after confirmation, so the next transaction I build already knows to use the next value regardless of what's actually confirmed yet. That turns a race condition into a simple sequential counter.
commonMistakes: Letting each transaction independently fetch 'the next nonce' from the provider when sent concurrently
Waiting for a transaction to confirm before incrementing the local nonce counter, rather than incrementing immediately on send
Not recognizing 'replacement underpriced' as a symptom of a duplicate nonce, not insufficient gas
Treating this as a network/node problem rather than an application-level nonce management bug
keyPoints: Nonces must be sequential per address; fetching 'next nonce' per transaction concurrently causes collisions
Managing the nonce as local application state, incremented immediately on send, avoids the race
'Replacement underpriced' can be a symptom of accidental duplicate nonce usage, not just low gas price
This is an application-level bug, not a chain or provider issue

Correctly explains why concurrent sends trigger this
Proposes correct fix: locally managed, immediately-incremented nonce

questions.title: A User's Session Breaks After Switching Wallet Accounts
questions.prompt: A user signs in with SIWE using one wallet address, gets a valid session, then switches accounts inside their wallet extension without logging out -- and your backend keeps treating requests as if they're still from the original address. What's wrong, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The session the backend issued after the original SIWE verification is tied to the address that was verified at that moment, and nothing about switching accounts in a wallet extension automatically invalidates or updates that session -- the backend has no way to know the wallet's active account changed unless the frontend specifically detects and reports it. The fix has two parts: the frontend should listen for the wallet provider's `accountsChanged` event and, on detecting a change, treat the existing session as invalid immediately (clearing it client-side and prompting re-authentication) rather than silently continuing to send requests under the stale session; and the backend's session should genuinely be scoped to the one address that was verified, never silently reinterpreted for a different address without a fresh signature.
questions.professionalAnswer: The session cookie or token my backend issued is bound to the address it actually verified via SIWE at that moment -- it has zero visibility into what the user's wallet extension is doing after that point, so a silent account switch inside the extension doesn't automatically tell my backend anything changed. That's a frontend responsibility: the wallet provider fires an accountsChanged event specifically for this, and my frontend needs to be listening for it and treating that as 'the current session is no longer valid for whichever address is now active,' forcing a fresh sign-in rather than quietly continuing to act as the old address. On the backend side, I'd make sure the session is genuinely scoped to the one verified address and there's no code path that would let it get silently reassigned without a new signature actually proving control of the new address.
commonMistakes: Assuming the backend can somehow detect a wallet account switch without the frontend reporting it
Not listening for the wallet provider's accountsChanged event on the frontend
Letting a session silently continue to represent an address that was never re-verified
Not forcing a fresh sign-in/signature after detecting an account switch
keyPoints: A session is bound to the address verified at sign-in; the backend has no visibility into later wallet changes
The frontend must listen for the wallet provider's accountsChanged event
Detecting a switch should invalidate the stale session and prompt re-authentication
A session should never be silently reassigned to a different address without a fresh verified signature

questions.title: A Subgraph Returns Stale or Missing Data
questions.prompt: Your frontend queries a deployed subgraph for recent events, but the data it returns is missing the last several minutes of on-chain activity, even though the chain itself clearly has newer blocks. What's the likely cause, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: A subgraph has to actually process every block to extract matching events into its own indexed database, and that processing lags behind the chain's head by some amount -- the first thing to check is the subgraph's own sync status (most hosting services, including The Graph's own tooling, expose a 'current indexed block' versus the chain's latest block), which immediately tells you whether this is simple indexing lag or something else. If the subgraph appears stuck far behind (not just a few blocks, but not advancing at all), the next likely cause is a mapping handler throwing an error on a specific block's data and halting further indexing -- checking the subgraph's own logs/error status for a failed handler is the next step. The fix depends on which: normal lag just needs time (or a faster-syncing node source), while a handler error needs a code fix and a redeploy, which for many subgraph implementations requires a full resync from the start.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I check is the subgraph's own indexing status versus the chain's actual head block -- there's almost always a way to query 'what block has this subgraph processed up to,' and comparing that against the chain's latest block tells me immediately whether I'm looking at ordinary indexing lag or something actually broken. If it's lagging by a reasonable, shrinking amount, that's probably just normal -- a subgraph has to process every block itself, it's not instant. If it's stuck and not moving at all, that's a different story -- usually a mapping handler threw an error on some specific block's event data and indexing halted right there. I'd check the subgraph's logs for that specific error. If it's a handler bug, the annoying part is that fixing it and redeploying often means a full resync from the beginning for a lot of subgraph setups, which is worth knowing up front so I'm not surprised by how long the fix takes.

Not checking the subgraph's own sync status (indexed block vs. chain head) as the first diagnostic step
Missing that a mapping handler error can halt indexing entirely rather than just slowing it
Not anticipating that fixing a handler bug may require a full resync, not just a quick redeploy

Checking indexed block vs. chain head distinguishes normal lag from a stuck/broken indexer
A mapping handler error on a specific block can halt indexing entirely
Fixing a handler bug often requires a full resync for many subgraph setups

questions.title: transferFrom Keeps Reverting Despite a Visible Allowance
questions.prompt: A user calls `approve` on an ERC-20 token, confirms the allowance is set correctly by reading `allowance()`, but then a contract's `transferFrom` call on their behalf still reverts. What are the likely causes, and how would you narrow it down?
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm which three addresses actually matter here: the token owner, the spender the allowance was granted to, and the address the contract is actually using when it calls transferFrom -- a very common cause is simply that the contract calling transferFrom isn't the same address the allowance was granted to (e.g. the frontend approved one contract address but the backend/contract logic calls through a different, perhaps newer, deployed address). Second, re-check the allowance using the exact spender address the failing call is using, not just 'an' allowance -- allowance() takes both owner and spender and a mismatch there looks like 'an allowance exists' while actually being insufficient or nonexistent for this specific spender. Third, confirm the owner's actual token balance is still sufficient at call time -- an allowance can exceed the owner's current balance, and transferFrom will revert on insufficient balance even with a technically valid allowance.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I check is whether the spender address the allowance was actually granted to is the exact address making the transferFrom call -- it's really common for a frontend to have approved one contract address, and then the actual call comes from a different address, maybe because of a redeploy or a proxy layer, and allowance() for the right owner/spender pair would show zero even though 'an allowance' looks like it was set for something. Second, I re-run allowance(owner, spender) with the exact pair the failing transaction is using, not just trusting an earlier check -- because a mismatch there is invisible unless I check that specific pair. Third, I check the owner's actual current balance, since an approved allowance doesn't guarantee the owner still holds enough tokens to cover it -- transferFrom checks both allowance and balance, and either one being insufficient causes the same kind of revert.

Checking 'an' allowance exists without re-verifying the specific owner/spender pair the failing call uses
Not checking the owner's current token balance separately from the allowance itself
Assuming a visible nonzero allowance rules out an allowance-related cause entirely

questions.title: A Multisig Transaction Isn't Executing Despite Enough Confirmations
questions.prompt: A multi-signature wallet contract requires 2-of-3 owner confirmations to execute a transaction. Two owners have confirmed, but calling execute still reverts. How would you figure out why?
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm the confirmations were actually recorded against the exact transaction being executed -- multisig contracts typically index pending transactions by an id, and a common mistake is confirming one transaction id while attempting to execute a different one (e.g. after resubmitting a transaction with changed parameters, which usually gets a new id). Second, check whether the contract's execute function has additional guards beyond the confirmation count -- many multisig implementations also check that the transaction hasn't already been executed (to prevent double execution), or that it hasn't expired/been revoked, and any of these would cause a revert independent of confirmation count. Third, verify the confirming addresses are actually recognized as owners by the contract's current state -- if ownership was ever changed, a 'confirmation' from a since-removed owner wouldn't count toward the threshold even if it was recorded earlier.
questions.professionalAnswer: First I'd check that both confirmations are actually attached to the exact transaction id being executed -- it's easy to confirm, then resubmit with a tweak that generates a new id, and end up confirming one id while trying to execute another. Then I'd look at what else execute actually checks beyond the raw confirmation count -- a lot of multisig implementations also guard against double-execution with an 'already executed' flag, or have an expiration/revocation path, and any of those would cause exactly this kind of revert regardless of how many confirmations exist. Last, I'd make sure both confirming addresses are still recognized as current owners by the contract -- if the owner set changed since a confirmation was recorded, that old confirmation might not count toward the threshold anymore depending on how the contract tracks it.

Overlooking an 'already executed' or expiration/revocation guard as the actual revert cause
Assuming confirmation count alone is sufficient without checking other execute() guards
Not verifying confirming addresses are still recognized as current owners

questions.title: Where the Line Actually Falls Between On-Chain and Off-Chain
questions.prompt: When you're designing a dApp, how do you actually decide what logic belongs in the smart contract versus what belongs in an off-chain backend? Walk through the reasoning, not just a rule of thumb.
questions.modelAnswer: The contract should hold only what genuinely needs the blockchain's specific guarantees: trustless execution nobody (including the app's own operator) can unilaterally alter, verifiable state that users can audit themselves, and the actual custody or transfer of on-chain assets. Everything else -- anything that benefits from being fast, cheap, flexible, or private, and doesn't need those guarantees -- belongs off-chain: indexing historical data for fast queries (the chain itself is a poor database to query directly), listening for events and reacting to them, calling external APIs or oracles, managing user sessions, sending notifications, rendering a UI. The reasoning isn't 'put as little as possible on-chain to save gas' as the primary driver (though that's a real secondary benefit) -- it's that on-chain logic is expensive to change, expensive to run, and visible to everyone, so it should be reserved for the specific things that actually require those tradeoffs.
questions.professionalAnswer: My actual question isn't 'what's cheapest,' it's 'what genuinely needs the chain's guarantees.' If something needs to be trustless -- nobody, including me as the operator, should be able to quietly change the outcome -- or it needs to be the actual custody/transfer of an on-chain asset, that belongs in the contract, full stop, because that's the one thing a backend can't give you. Everything else is a backend's job, and honestly a backend does it better: querying history fast (the chain is a genuinely bad database to query directly, which is the whole reason indexers like The Graph exist), reacting to events, calling external oracles, managing a user's session, sending them a notification. Gas cost is a real factor too, but it's downstream of this -- once I know something has to be on-chain because it needs those specific guarantees, then I think about how to implement it efficiently; I don't start from 'minimize gas' and work backward to decide what belongs where.

Putting logic on-chain that would work fine off-chain, just because it feels more 'decentralized'
Underestimating how much normal dApp functionality (indexing, notifications, sessions) genuinely belongs off-chain
Not identifying trustlessness and asset custody as the specific things only the chain can actually provide

Indexing, event reaction, oracle calls, sessions, and notifications are normal off-chain responsibilities
The chain is a poor database for querying; that's why off-chain indexing exists at all
Gas efficiency is a real secondary concern, downstream of deciding what must be on-chain in the first place

questions.title: Why a dApp Backend Can't Just Query the Chain Directly
questions.prompt: A product manager asks why you need 'all this indexing infrastructure' instead of just having the backend ask the blockchain directly for things like 'show me this user's last 50 transactions.' How do you explain the actual architectural reason?
questions.modelAnswer: A blockchain node exposes narrow, specific lookups -- balance at an address, a transaction by its hash, logs matching a known contract and event signature within a block range -- but it has no general-purpose query engine; there's no efficient native way to ask 'every event involving this user across contracts, sorted by time, paginated,' because that would require scanning potentially the entire chain's history on every request. An indexer (a custom service, or a managed one like The Graph) solves this by continuously processing new blocks as they arrive, extracting the relevant events into its own purpose-built database (often relational or graph-structured) that's actually optimized for the queries the application needs, so a request like 'this user's last 50 transactions' becomes a fast, ordinary database query against pre-processed data instead of an expensive chain scan done fresh every time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer is that a node is built to answer very specific, narrow questions fast -- 'what's this address's balance,' 'what's in this specific transaction' -- but it has nothing like a real query engine. Asking it 'show me this user's last 50 transactions across these contracts, sorted and paginated' isn't a thing it can answer efficiently; that's effectively asking it to scan a huge amount of history on the spot, every single time someone loads a page. An indexer flips that: it watches new blocks as they come in, pulls out exactly the events we care about, and stores them in a normal database that's actually designed for the queries our app needs. By the time a user asks for their last 50 transactions, that's just an ordinary, fast database query against data we already processed ahead of time, not a live scan of the chain.

Not explaining that a node's native lookups are narrow and specific, not general-purpose
Describing an indexer as merely a cache rather than explaining it continuously processes and restructures data for querying

questions.title: The Graph's Subgraph Model, at the Architecture Level
questions.prompt: How does The Graph's subgraph model actually fit into a dApp's architecture -- what runs where, and what's the relationship between the schema, the mapping handlers, and the deployed subgraph your frontend queries?
questions.modelAnswer: A subgraph definition has two core pieces authored by the developer: a GraphQL schema describing the entities (shapes of data) the subgraph will expose, and mapping handlers (written in AssemblyScript) that run whenever a specified contract emits a matching event, transforming that raw event data into instances of the schema's entities. Once deployed, The Graph's indexing infrastructure (or a self-hosted equivalent) continuously processes new blocks, triggers the relevant mapping handler for each matching event, and persists the resulting entities into its own store. The frontend (or backend) then queries the deployed subgraph's GraphQL endpoint directly -- it never talks to the chain or the mapping handlers at query time; those already did their job when the event was originally processed. The architectural benefit is that the expensive, structural work (deciding how raw events become queryable entities) happens once, continuously, as new data arrives, and querying afterward is cheap and fast.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about it: I write two things, a schema that defines what entities look like (a 'Transfer' entity with from, to, amount, timestamp, say), and mapping handlers that get triggered every time a matching event fires on the contract I'm watching, and whose job is to take that raw event and turn it into an entity matching my schema. Once that's deployed, the actual indexing runs continuously in the background -- new block comes in, matching event found, handler runs, entity gets stored -- completely separate from anyone actually querying the data. My frontend then just hits the subgraph's GraphQL endpoint directly, like any other API, and it's fast because all the real transformation work already happened asynchronously as events occurred, not at query time. That separation -- continuous background processing versus on-demand querying -- is really the whole architectural point.

Not distinguishing the schema (entity shape) from the mapping handlers (event-to-entity transformation logic)
Implying the frontend talks to the chain directly when querying a subgraph
Missing the architectural benefit of separating continuous processing from on-demand querying

questions.title: Custom Indexer vs. Managed Indexing Service: the Real Tradeoff
questions.prompt: You need to index on-chain data for a new dApp. What's the actual tradeoff between building a custom indexer yourself versus using a managed service like The Graph, and what would make you choose one over the other?
questions.modelAnswer: A managed service like The Graph gets you to a working, queryable index much faster -- you write a schema and mapping handlers in its specific framework, deploy, and the infrastructure (block processing, storage, the query API) is handled for you, at the cost of working within that framework's constraints (its query language's capabilities, its specific event-processing model, and reliance on either a hosted or decentralized network you don't fully control). A custom indexer (a service you write yourself, processing events and writing to a database of your own choosing) gives full control over data modeling, query capabilities, and infrastructure, at the cost of building and operating that infrastructure yourself -- reorg handling, backfill/resync logic, uptime, and scaling are now entirely your responsibility. The real decision point is usually whether the application's query needs fit comfortably within a managed service's model: if they do, the time saved is substantial; if the application needs query patterns, latency guarantees, or data transformations the managed service's framework doesn't support well, a custom indexer becomes the better fit despite the extra operational burden.
questions.professionalAnswer: A managed service gets me from zero to a working, queryable index really fast -- I write a schema and some handlers in their framework, deploy, and I'm not the one worrying about reorg handling or keeping an indexing process alive and caught up. The tradeoff is I'm working inside their model: their query language, their event-processing assumptions, whatever their hosted or decentralized network's reliability characteristics are. A custom indexer flips that completely -- I own the whole pipeline, which means total control over how data is modeled and queried, but it also means I own reorg handling, backfills, uptime, and scaling, none of which are free. My actual decision point is whether my query needs fit comfortably in the managed service's model. If I just need 'give me this entity filtered and paginated this way,' a managed service is clearly the right call. If I need something that framework genuinely can't express well, or I need guarantees about latency or data residency it can't give me, that's when building my own starts making sense, even knowing it's more work.
commonMistakes: Treating a managed service as strictly easier with no real constraints
Underestimating the operational burden (reorg handling, backfill, uptime) a custom indexer takes on
Not identifying query-pattern fit as the actual deciding factor
Framing this as a purely technical decision rather than a genuine cost/control tradeoff
keyPoints: A managed service offers speed to a working index at the cost of working within its framework's constraints
A custom indexer offers full control at the cost of owning reorg handling, backfill, uptime, and scaling
The deciding factor is usually whether the app's query needs fit the managed service's model
This is a genuine cost/control tradeoff, not a simple 'better' choice either way

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the managed-service tradeoff
Correctly describes the custom-indexer tradeoff, including operational burden
Gives a correct, concrete deciding factor
Balanced, realistic framing of the tradeoff
