questions.title: Designing a Reliable Event Listener Service
questions.prompt: You're designing a backend service whose only job is to listen for a specific contract event and trigger a downstream action (like sending a notification) each time it fires. What architectural decisions make this service actually reliable in production, versus a naive version that just subscribes and reacts?
questions.modelAnswer: A naive listener that just subscribes via WebSocket and reacts to each event as it arrives has several real gaps: it has no record of which events it's already processed, so a restart (deployment, crash, dropped connection) either reprocesses old events or silently misses whatever happened while it was down; it has no defense against triggering the downstream action twice for the same event (from a dropped-and-reconnected subscription re-delivering, or from a chain reorg); and it treats a 'new' event as immediately final despite reorg risk. A reliable design persists the last block it has fully processed, so on restart it can resume by querying `eth_getLogs` for anything missed since that block rather than relying solely on a live subscription; it records which specific events (by transaction hash + log index) have already triggered the downstream action, making that action idempotent against being re-delivered; and it applies a confirmation-depth buffer before treating an event as final, to reduce reorg-related double-processing or false triggers.
questions.professionalAnswer: The naive version -- just subscribe and react -- breaks in a few predictable ways once it's actually running in production. First, it has no memory: if it restarts for any reason, it has no idea what it already handled versus what happened while it was down, so it either double-fires or silently misses things. Second, it has no protection against processing the same event twice, which can genuinely happen with a dropped-and-reconnected subscription or a reorg. My actual design persists the last block I've confirmed fully processed, so on startup I can backfill anything I might have missed with a direct eth_getLogs query instead of just trusting the live subscription picked up everything. I also key each processed event by its transaction hash plus log index and check that key before triggering the downstream action, so even if I somehow see the same event twice, the action itself only fires once. And I wait for a small confirmation buffer before treating an event as final at all, specifically to avoid acting on something that gets reorged away moments later.
commonMistakes: Designing a listener with no persisted 'last processed block,' making restarts unreliable
No idempotency protection against processing the same event more than once
No backfill mechanism to catch events that occurred while the service was down
Treating a freshly seen event as immediately final with no confirmation buffer
keyPoints: Persisting the last fully processed block enables safe backfill on restart
Keying processed events by tx hash + log index makes the downstream action idempotent
A confirmation-depth buffer reduces reorg-related double-processing or false triggers
A naive subscribe-and-react design has real gaps around restarts, duplicates, and reorgs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the real gaps in a naive listener design
Proposes persisted last-processed-block + backfill on restart
Proposes idempotency keying for the downstream action
Mentions a confirmation-depth buffer for reorg safety

questions.title: Chainlink Automation vs. Running Your Own Cron Job
questions.prompt: You need a smart contract function to be called automatically whenever a certain condition becomes true on-chain. What's the architectural difference between using Chainlink Automation for this versus just running your own backend cron job that calls the function?
questions.modelAnswer: A self-run cron job is a centralized, single point of failure and trust: your backend has to stay online, has to hold (or have access to) a funded wallet to pay gas for the triggering transaction, and if your service goes down, the condition can become true and nothing calls the function until you notice and intervene. Chainlink Automation decentralizes exactly that responsibility -- a network of independent node operators continuously checks the condition (via a `checkUpkeep` function you define) and whichever node notices it's true submits the triggering transaction, funded from a prepaid upkeep balance you maintain rather than your own backend's wallet. The architectural tradeoff is giving up some control (you're relying on Chainlink's network and its specific upkeep registration/funding model) in exchange for removing your own backend's uptime as a single point of failure for a time- or condition-sensitive on-chain action.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest difference is where the single point of failure lives. With my own cron job, it's my backend -- if it's down, or its wallet runs out of gas money, or there's a bug, the on-chain action that was supposed to fire automatically just... doesn't, and I might not notice for a while. Chainlink Automation moves that responsibility onto a decentralized network of node operators who are themselves checking my condition via a checkUpkeep function and competing to be the one who submits the triggering transaction when it's true, funded from an upkeep balance I keep topped up rather than from my own backend's wallet. The tradeoff is real, though -- I'm now depending on Chainlink's network and its specific registration and funding model instead of infrastructure I fully control. For anything where 'this absolutely must fire reliably even if my own servers have a bad day' matters, that tradeoff is usually worth it.
commonMistakes: Not identifying backend uptime as the actual single point of failure in a self-run cron approach
Describing Chainlink Automation without mentioning the checkUpkeep/upkeep-funding model
Treating the managed option as strictly better with no tradeoff at all
Not mentioning gas funding as a real operational concern in either approach
keyPoints: A self-run cron job makes your backend's uptime and wallet funding a single point of failure
Chainlink Automation decentralizes condition-checking and triggering across independent node operators
checkUpkeep defines the condition; triggering is funded from a prepaid upkeep balance
The tradeoff is reduced control/self-sufficiency in exchange for removing your own uptime as the bottleneck

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the single-point-of-failure risk in a self-run cron job
Correctly explains Chainlink Automation's decentralized triggering model
Correctly frames the real tradeoff rather than declaring one strictly better
Clear, accurate terminology

questions.title: How Gasless Transactions Actually Work, Architecturally
questions.prompt: A product wants users to be able to interact with a dApp without needing ETH in their wallet to pay gas. At an architectural level, how does a relayer-based gasless transaction flow actually work, and what trust assumption does it introduce?
questions.modelAnswer: Instead of the user submitting a transaction directly (which requires them to pay gas from their own wallet), the user signs a message describing the intended action off-chain (which costs nothing, since signing isn't a transaction), and submits that signed message to a relayer service rather than to the chain. The relayer -- a backend service with its own funded wallet -- wraps that signed message into an actual transaction, pays the gas itself, and submits it on-chain, typically through a contract designed to verify the user's signature and execute the intended action as if the user had called it directly (a 'forwarder' or meta-transaction pattern). The trust assumption this introduces is real: the user is now depending on the relayer to actually submit their transaction in a timely way (or at all), and depending on whoever operates the relayer to keep it funded and honest -- the user's signed intent can't be forged into a different action, but it can be delayed or withheld by a relayer that misbehaves or goes down, which is a meaningfully different trust profile than a user submitting their own transaction directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core move is separating 'expressing intent' from 'paying for and submitting the transaction.' The user signs a message off-chain describing what they want to do -- that costs them nothing, since a signature isn't a transaction -- and hands that signed message to a relayer instead of submitting it themselves. The relayer is a backend service with its own funded wallet that takes that signed intent, wraps it into a real transaction, pays the gas, and submits it on-chain through a contract built to verify the signature and execute exactly what the user authorized. What I'm honest with myself about is the trust assumption this adds: the user's intent can't be twisted into something else because it's cryptographically signed, but it absolutely can be delayed or just never submitted if the relayer is down, broke, or acting badly. That's a real dependency I'm introducing that a direct, self-paid transaction doesn't have, and it's worth being upfront about that with whoever's deciding whether this UX tradeoff is worth it.
commonMistakes: Describing gasless transactions as if gas disappears, rather than being paid by the relayer
Not explaining that the user signs an off-chain message rather than submitting a transaction directly
Missing the forwarder/meta-transaction contract's role in verifying the signature on-chain
Failing to identify the real trust/dependency risk the relayer introduces
keyPoints: The user signs an off-chain message expressing intent, which costs nothing and isn't itself a transaction
A relayer wraps that signed intent into a real transaction and pays the gas from its own wallet
A forwarder/meta-transaction contract verifies the signature on-chain and executes the authorized action
The user now depends on the relayer's availability and honesty to actually submit the transaction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the off-chain signed-intent step
Correctly explains the relayer's role and the forwarder/meta-tx pattern
Correctly identifies the trust assumption introduced
Clear, accurate terminology

questions.title: Designing Shared Control With a Multisig Wallet
questions.prompt: A team wants to control a contract's treasury funds such that no single person can move money alone. Architecturally, how does a multisig wallet actually achieve that, and what design decisions (threshold, owner set) matter most?
questions.modelAnswer: A multisig contract holds funds itself (rather than any individual's wallet holding them), and any transfer out requires a proposed transaction to collect a minimum number (the threshold) of confirmations from a defined set of owner addresses before it can actually execute -- the contract enforces this on-chain, so no single owner's private key, however compromised or malicious, is sufficient on its own to move funds. The two defining design decisions are the owner set (who specifically has signing authority, and how that set can itself be changed -- ideally also requiring multisig approval, to prevent a single compromised key from unilaterally adding a new, malicious owner) and the threshold (how many of those owners must agree) -- a threshold too low undermines the whole point (e.g. 1-of-3 is barely different from a single key), while a threshold too high (e.g. requiring every single owner, with no tolerance for one being unavailable) risks the fund becoming inaccessible if even one owner loses key access or becomes unreachable. A common balance for a small team is something like 2-of-3 or 3-of-5, explicitly trading off security against the practical risk of losing availability.
questions.professionalAnswer: The actual mechanism is that the money lives in the contract itself, not in any one person's wallet, and the contract's own logic refuses to move anything out until enough of the designated owners have separately confirmed a specific proposed transaction -- that's enforced on-chain, so there's no social or off-chain workaround; it's a hard requirement in the code. The two things I'd think hardest about designing this are who's actually in the owner set, including how that set itself gets changed later (ideally that change also requires multisig approval, so a single compromised key can't just add itself a friend), and what threshold to require. Too low and you haven't really solved the single-point-of-failure problem -- 1-of-3 isn't meaningfully different from one key. Too high, like requiring all N owners with zero tolerance for anyone being unreachable, and you risk permanently locking the funds if even one person loses their key or goes dark. For a small team, something like 2-of-3 is a pretty deliberate middle ground: real protection against one compromised or malicious actor, but enough slack that one person being unavailable doesn't brick the treasury.
commonMistakes: Not explaining that the contract itself holds the funds, enforcing the threshold on-chain rather than socially
Treating the threshold choice as unimportant, missing the too-low/too-high tradeoff
Not considering how the owner set itself can be changed, and the risk of that being insufficiently protected
Giving no concrete reasoning for a specific threshold choice
keyPoints: The multisig contract itself holds funds and enforces the confirmation threshold on-chain
The owner set defines who has signing authority, and its own modification should require multisig approval too
A threshold too low undermines shared-control security; too high risks locking funds if an owner is unavailable
A balanced threshold (e.g. 2-of-3, 3-of-5) deliberately trades security against availability risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the on-chain enforcement mechanism
Correctly discusses the owner-set design consideration
Correctly discusses the threshold tradeoff (too low vs. too high)
Gives a concrete, reasoned threshold recommendation

questions.title: Modeling an Auction Contract's State Machine
questions.prompt: You're designing an English auction contract for NFTs -- bidding, outbidding, and eventually ending the auction. How would you think about this as a state machine, and what state transitions are the ones most likely to introduce bugs if handled carelessly?
questions.modelAnswer: An English auction naturally has a small number of states -- not-yet-started, open for bidding, and ended -- and the contract's functions should each only be callable in the state(s) where they're actually valid (bidding only while open, ending only once, withdrawal of outbid funds available any time after being outbid). The transitions most likely to introduce bugs are: accepting a new highest bid while correctly returning the previous highest bidder's funds (getting the ordering wrong here is exactly the reentrancy risk seen in the real English-auction lesson -- the refund to the outbid bidder needs to follow checks-effects-interactions, updating the new highest bidder/amount before sending anything back to the old one); and the single transition into 'ended,' which needs a guard against being triggered twice (a double-end could transfer the NFT or funds out twice) and against being triggered before the auction's actual end condition (time elapsed, or an explicit end call by the right party) is genuinely met.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as three real states: not started, open, ended -- and every function needs an explicit check for which state it's actually valid in, rather than assuming callers will behave. The transition that worries me most is accepting a new highest bid, because that's exactly where the course's own reentrancy lesson lives -- when a new bid comes in, I have to update who the current highest bidder is and refund the previous one, and if I send that refund before updating my own bookkeeping, I've opened the same reentrancy door as any other refund-before-state-update bug. The other transition I'm careful with is ending the auction -- that should only be reachable once, with a flag or state check that makes a second call to end() a no-op or an explicit revert, because an auction that can be 'ended' twice could transfer the NFT or release funds twice. And ending itself needs its own precondition -- either enough time has genuinely passed, or whoever's allowed to end it early is actually who they claim to be.
commonMistakes: Not treating the contract's valid states explicitly, allowing functions to be called in states where they shouldn't be
Refunding the previous highest bidder before updating the new highest bidder's state, risking reentrancy
Not guarding the ending transition against being triggered more than once
Not validating the actual end condition (time elapsed, correct caller) before allowing the auction to end
keyPoints: An English auction has a small number of valid states; functions should check which state they're valid in
Accepting a new bid and refunding the previous bidder is a real reentrancy risk if ordered incorrectly
The ending transition must be guarded against being triggered more than once
The ending transition's precondition (time elapsed, or correct caller) must be genuinely validated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the contract as a small explicit state machine
Correctly identifies the new-bid/refund transition's reentrancy risk
Correctly identifies the double-ending risk and its fix
Mentions validating the actual end precondition

questions.title: Choosing Between ERC-20 and ERC-721 for a New Project
questions.prompt: A client wants to tokenize something -- say, membership passes for a community. How do you reason through whether ERC-20 or ERC-721 is the right standard, architecturally, for what they're actually describing?
questions.modelAnswer: The deciding question is whether individual units of the thing being tokenized are interchangeable or distinguishable. ERC-20 models fungible value -- every unit is identical and only the quantity matters, which fits currencies, points, or voting weight. ERC-721 models non-fungible, individually distinct items -- each token has its own id and can carry its own metadata (which specific membership tier, when it was issued, what perks are attached) distinguishing it from every other token of the same contract, which fits anything where 'which specific one you hold' matters, not just 'how many.' Membership passes usually fit ERC-721 rather than ERC-20 specifically because real memberships tend to have individual identity -- a specific tier, a specific join date, perhaps transfer restrictions or specific perks tied to that one pass -- that would be awkward or impossible to represent if every pass were just an interchangeable unit of the same fungible token.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question is always: are individual units of this thing actually interchangeable, or does which specific one you hold matter? ERC-20 is built for 'only the quantity matters' -- a currency, a point balance, voting weight, where token #4,001 is in every way identical to token #4,002. ERC-721 is built for the opposite -- every token is its own distinct thing with its own id and potentially its own metadata, so token #4,001 and #4,002 can be meaningfully different. For membership passes specifically, I'd push back if someone suggested ERC-20, because real memberships almost always carry individual identity -- which tier someone has, when they joined, specific perks attached to that one pass -- and an ERC-20 balance has no native way to represent 'this specific unit is different from that one.' ERC-721 gives each pass its own identity and metadata slot, which is what the actual use case needs, even if it costs a bit more in gas and complexity than a simple fungible balance would.
commonMistakes: Not identifying fungibility (interchangeable vs. distinguishable units) as the actual deciding factor
Choosing based on familiarity or hype rather than what the use case structurally needs
Not recognizing that membership passes typically need individual identity/metadata, which ERC-20 can't represent
Treating this as a purely technical choice without considering what the client's actual requirement implies
keyPoints: ERC-20 models fungible value where only quantity matters; ERC-721 models distinguishable, individually identified items
The deciding question is whether individual units are interchangeable or need their own identity/metadata
Membership passes typically need individual identity (tier, join date, perks), fitting ERC-721
The right choice follows from what the use case structurally requires, not familiarity or trend

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly articulates the fungible vs. non-fungible deciding question
Correctly maps the membership-pass use case to ERC-721
Gives concrete reasoning, not just a naming of standards
Clear, accurate terminology

questions.title: Explaining Why a Deployed Contract Can't Just Be Patched
questions.prompt: A non-technical product manager is frustrated that a bug found in a live smart contract 'can't just be fixed with a quick patch like a normal website.' How do you explain this to them in a way that actually lands, and how do you frame the path forward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids jargon-heavy over-explanation and instead reaches for a relatable analogy -- something like 'once this is deployed, it's more like a vending machine bolted to a wall than a website; we can't sneak in and swap a part while it's running, we can only build a new one and move people over to it' -- before getting into any technical detail. It then concretely explains the actual path forward: assess real impact and urgency, decide whether a pause mechanism (if one exists) should be used right now, and scope what a fixed redeployment and migration actually involves, giving the PM a realistic timeline rather than vague reassurance. The goal is making the PM an informed partner in the decision, not just absorbing their frustration quietly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with the analogy before any technical detail, because 'it's literally impossible to edit the code at that address' lands a lot better as 'think of it like a vending machine already bolted to the wall -- we can't open it up and swap a part while it's running, we can only build a new one and move everyone's access over to that' than as a lecture about immutability. Once that clicks, I'd walk them through what actually happens next in concrete terms: how bad is this bug really, is there a pause switch we should hit right now, and here's a realistic estimate for building, testing, and migrating to a fixed version. What I'm trying to avoid is the PM walking away either panicked or dismissive -- I want them to actually understand why 'just patch it' isn't on the table, and to be an informed part of deciding what happens next.
commonMistakes: Over-explaining with blockchain jargon instead of starting with a relatable analogy
Letting the PM walk away still expecting a quick patch is somehow possible
Not giving a concrete, realistic next-steps plan with a timeline
Being purely reassuring without being honest about real impact or urgency
keyPoints: Leads with a relatable analogy before technical explanation
Makes clear a deployed contract genuinely cannot be edited in place
Gives a concrete, realistic path forward (impact assessment, pause if available, redeployment plan)
Treats the PM as an informed partner in the decision, not someone to just reassure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses a clear, accurate analogy for a non-technical audience
Correctly conveys that the deployed contract cannot be patched in place
Gives a concrete, realistic path forward
Communicates honestly without being alarmist or dismissive

questions.title: A Team Lead Pushes to Skip a Security Audit to Hit a Launch Date
questions.prompt: Your team lead wants to launch a contract handling real user funds on the original date, which means skipping the external security audit that was originally planned. How do you handle this disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just refuse or escalate dramatically, but also doesn't quietly go along with a decision it believes is genuinely risky. The right first step is making the actual risk concrete and specific rather than vaguely objecting -- naming the categories of bugs an audit is specifically designed to catch (reentrancy, access control gaps, integer issues) that internal review is less likely to find, and being honest that 'it compiled and passed our own tests' is a different bar than 'an independent security specialist reviewed it.' If the lead still wants to proceed after hearing that clearly, the answer should describe either accepting the decision while documenting the known risk, or escalating to whoever owns the actual risk tolerance for funds at stake (not undermining the lead, but making sure the tradeoff is made by someone with the authority and context to own that call) -- not silently complying with a decision that could lose users real money.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say 'no, I refuse to launch without an audit,' but I also wouldn't quietly go along with it if I actually believe it's a real risk to user funds. I'd make the risk specific rather than vague -- audits are specifically good at catching exactly the kinds of things, reentrancy, access control holes, that our own internal testing is structurally less likely to catch, because we're testing the behavior we expect, not actively trying to break our own contract the way an adversarial auditor would. I'd lay that out clearly and let my lead make an informed call with that in front of them. If they still want to launch on schedule after hearing that, and this is genuinely about funds at risk, I'd want this escalated to whoever actually owns that risk -- isn't a decision I'd want made quietly between the two of us if real money is on the line. That's not about undermining my lead, it's about making sure the person with the authority to accept that risk is the one actually accepting it.
commonMistakes: Either silently complying with a risky decision or flatly refusing without explaining the real risk
Making a vague objection ('this feels risky') instead of naming specifically what an audit catches
Not escalating to whoever actually owns risk tolerance when real user funds are at stake
Framing this as undermining the team lead rather than ensuring an informed decision
keyPoints: Makes the specific risk concrete (what an audit catches that internal testing typically misses)
Avoids both silent compliance and dramatic refusal
Escalates to whoever owns risk tolerance when real funds are at stake, if the disagreement persists
Frames the goal as an informed decision, not undermining the lead's authority

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Articulates the specific risk an audit addresses, not a vague objection
Avoids silent compliance with a decision believed to be genuinely risky
Describes an appropriate escalation path when funds are at stake
Frames this professionally, not as undermining the lead

questions.title: You Introduced a Bug During a Live Demo
questions.prompt: During a live demo to stakeholders, you deploy what turns out to be a buggy version of a contract to a testnet, and a function clearly misbehaves in front of everyone. How do you handle that moment, and what do you do afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the in-the-moment response and the follow-up as two separate things. In the moment, the right move is a brief, calm, honest acknowledgment -- naming that this is a bug in the demo build, not a fundamental flaw in the approach, and moving on rather than spiraling into a long live debugging session in front of the audience, which rarely goes well and erodes confidence further. Afterward, the actual work is diagnosing and fixing the real cause, being specific with stakeholders about what went wrong and what's been corrected (not vague reassurance), and considering whether the demo process itself needs a change (e.g. always demoing a known-good, tagged commit rather than whatever's currently on a branch) to reduce the chance of this recurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: In the room, I'd keep it short and honest -- something like 'that's not expected, this looks like a bug in today's build, let me note it and we'll come back to it' -- and then actually move on rather than trying to debug live in front of an audience, which almost always makes things worse and eats everyone's time. After the demo, the real work starts: actually find the root cause, fix it, and go back to whoever was in that room with something specific -- not 'it's fixed,' but 'here's what was actually wrong and here's what's different now.' I'd also look at why this happened in the first place -- if I demoed from a branch that wasn't actually tested end to end, the fix isn't just 'be more careful next time,' it's probably 'demos should always come from a specific tagged, verified build,' so the same mistake doesn't just repeat itself next time under different circumstances.
commonMistakes: Panicking or trying to debug live in front of the audience instead of acknowledging and moving on
Being vague or defensive about what happened instead of giving a specific follow-up explanation
Not identifying a process fix (e.g. demoing from a known-good build) to reduce recurrence
Treating the incident as purely embarrassing rather than an ordinary, recoverable mistake
keyPoints: In the moment: brief, calm, honest acknowledgment, then move on rather than live-debugging
Afterward: find the real root cause and follow up with specifics, not vague reassurance
Considers a process fix (demoing from a known-good, tagged build) to reduce recurrence
Treats the mistake professionally rather than defensively or as a crisis

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, calm in-the-moment response
Describes genuine follow-up diagnosis and a specific explanation afterward
Proposes a concrete process improvement to reduce recurrence
Professional, non-defensive tone throughout

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Teammate Over an Upgradeable Proxy Pattern
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to use an upgradeable proxy pattern for a new contract 'just in case we need to change something later,' but you think a simple, immutable contract is the better choice for this specific case. How do you work through that disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as a genuine technical tradeoff to work through together, not a battle to win. The substantive point to raise is that upgradeability isn't free -- it adds real complexity (proxy/implementation separation, storage layout constraints across upgrades, an admin key that itself becomes a security-critical single point of trust) and should be a deliberate choice justified by a specific, likely need to change logic later, not a default 'just in case' hedge. The right approach is asking the teammate directly what specific future change they're actually anticipating, and if there's a concrete, likely reason, factoring that into the decision honestly; if it's a vague general hedge, explaining the real cost of upgradeability and why a simpler, immutable, easier-to-audit contract might be the better choice here specifically, while remaining open to being convinced if they have a reason that wasn't yet stated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as something to actually work through rather than just asserting my preference. My real question for my teammate would be specific: what's the actual future change you're anticipating that makes upgradeability worth the cost here? Because upgradeability isn't free -- it adds real complexity, storage layout constraints across every future upgrade, and an admin key that becomes its own security-critical thing to protect, which is exactly the kind of extra attack surface that's worth avoiding unless there's a genuine, likely reason to need it. If they have a specific, credible reason, that changes my view and I'd want to factor it in honestly. If it's really just a general 'just in case' hedge with nothing concrete behind it, I'd want to make the real cost visible and suggest a simpler, immutable contract is probably the better tradeoff for this specific case -- while staying open that I might be missing something they haven't said yet.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a battle to win rather than a technical tradeoff to work through together
Not asking what specific future need the teammate is actually anticipating
Describing upgradeability as free, missing its real complexity and security costs
Being unwilling to reconsider if the teammate has a concrete, credible reason
keyPoints: Upgradeability adds real complexity and a new security-critical trust point (the admin key)
Asks what specific future need is actually being anticipated, rather than assuming 'just in case' is unfounded
Makes the real cost of upgradeability visible rather than dismissing the idea outright
Remains genuinely open to being convinced by a concrete, credible reason

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real costs of an upgradeable pattern
Describes asking for the teammate's specific reasoning rather than assuming
Frames the disagreement as collaborative, not adversarial
Shows genuine openness to being convinced

questions.title: A Client Is Shocked by Gas Costs After the Fact
questions.prompt: A client is upset that deploying and running their contract on Ethereum mainnet is costing far more in gas than they expected, and implies you should have warned them more clearly upfront. How do you handle this conversation?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't get defensive or immediately argue about who said what -- it acknowledges the client's frustration as legitimate regardless of exactly what was communicated before, then moves to being genuinely useful: breaking down specifically where the cost is coming from (deployment cost, a particular expensive function, transaction volume) rather than leaving it as a vague complaint, and presenting concrete options going forward -- optimizing the specific expensive operations, considering a cheaper L2 network if that fits the use case, or adjusting how often certain on-chain actions happen. It also honestly reflects on whether gas cost expectations were actually set clearly enough upfront, and commits to doing that more explicitly on this and future engagements, rather than relitigating exactly what was said before.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start by defending exactly what I did or didn't say upfront -- that conversation doesn't actually help the client right now, even if I think I was reasonably clear. I'd acknowledge the frustration is legitimate, then get useful fast: let's actually break down where the cost is coming from specifically, is it the deployment itself, is it one particular function being called a lot, is it just higher transaction volume than planned for. Once that's concrete, I can lay out real options -- optimizing the specific expensive parts, looking at whether an L2 actually fits their use case and would cut costs significantly, or changing how often certain actions happen on-chain versus batched. Separately, afterward, I'd be honest with myself about whether I actually set gas-cost expectations clearly enough at the start of this engagement, and if not, that's a real process fix for how I scope future projects, not something to argue about with this client right now.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive or arguing about exactly what was communicated before, instead of addressing the current problem
Leaving the cost complaint vague instead of breaking down specifically where it's coming from
Not offering concrete forward-looking options (optimization, L2, batching)
Not honestly reflecting on whether expectations were actually set clearly enough upfront
keyPoints: Acknowledges the client's frustration without getting defensive about prior communication
Breaks down specifically where the gas cost is actually coming from
Presents concrete forward-looking options (optimization, L2, reduced on-chain frequency)
Honestly reflects on whether expectations were set clearly enough, as a process improvement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively
Describes breaking the cost down into specific, concrete sources
Offers concrete, realistic forward-looking options
Shows honest self-reflection on expectation-setting

questions.title: Raising a Reentrancy Concern in a Teammate's Pull Request
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a teammate's pull request and spot what looks like a reentrancy vulnerability -- an external call before a balance update. How do you raise this in the review without it landing as an attack on their competence?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer focuses the comment on the specific code pattern and its concrete consequence, not on the person -- naming the exact lines, explaining mechanically what could go wrong (a malicious contract on the receiving end could re-enter before the balance update, draining funds), and proposing the concrete fix (reordering to checks-effects-interactions, or adding a reentrancy guard) rather than just flagging a vague concern. It treats this as a routine, expected part of reviewing contract code -- finding exactly this class of bug is specifically what careful review is for -- rather than a surprising failure on the author's part, and frames it collaboratively ('want to double check this ordering' rather than 'you made a mistake').
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the comment specific and mechanical rather than general -- pointing at the exact lines, saying something like 'this sends funds before updating the balance, which means a malicious contract on the receiving end could call back into this function before the balance is decremented and potentially drain more than intended -- want to reorder this to update the balance first, or add a reentrancy guard?' That's a comment about the code, not about them, and it comes with a concrete suggested fix rather than just a vague red flag. I'd also treat this as a completely normal part of reviewing contract code -- this exact pattern is one of the most well-known classes of smart contract bugs, catching it in review is the system working as intended, not a sign anyone did something unusually bad.
commonMistakes: Making the comment feel personal or accusatory rather than focused on the specific code
Flagging a vague 'this looks risky' without naming the specific lines and mechanism
Not proposing a concrete fix alongside the concern
Treating finding this bug as an unusual failure rather than a normal part of reviewing contract code
keyPoints: Focuses the comment on specific lines and the concrete mechanism, not the author
Explains exactly what could go wrong (reentrant call before balance update)
Proposes a concrete fix (reordering, or a reentrancy guard)
Frames finding this as normal, expected code review, not a personal failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Keeps the feedback specific to the code, not the person
Correctly explains the reentrancy mechanism being flagged
Proposes a concrete fix alongside the concern
Frames this as a normal part of review, not a personal criticism

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time

questions.title: A Dashboard Goes Live, and Immediately Something's Wrong
questions.prompt: Two days after a new regional revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region, which is obviously wrong. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while you're still figuring it out.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the investigation from the communication, and gets both moving in parallel rather than going silent until the fix is found. On investigation, the logical order is checking the environments closest to the symptom first: is this specific region's data actually present in the underlying source as of the relevant date, did the scheduled refresh for this model actually complete successfully (checking refresh history for errors), and does any report-level filter (RLS, a regional filter default) unintentionally exclude this region's rows. On communication, the mistake to avoid is going quiet until the root cause is fully found — the right move is an immediate, honest acknowledgment that specifically names what's being checked ("I've confirmed the issue and I'm checking whether it's a refresh failure or a filter problem, I'll update you within the hour") rather than either a vague "looking into it" or disappearing until there's a complete answer, since a specific update lets the regional manager decide what to do in the meantime (for example, whether to trust other numbers from the same report).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do two things essentially at the same time: start investigating, and send the regional manager something specific right away rather than going quiet until I have a full answer. On the investigation side, I'd work from the symptom outward — first checking refresh history to see whether last night's scheduled refresh for this model actually succeeded, since a failed or partial refresh is a really common cause of 'this one region looks wrong.' If the refresh is fine, I'd check whether the region's data is actually present in the source table for the relevant date, and then check whether any filter — RLS, a default slicer, anything report-level — is quietly excluding that region specifically. On the communication side, I'd send something concrete almost immediately, like 'I've confirmed something's wrong with the regional number, I'm checking whether it's a refresh issue or a filter issue right now, I'll have an update for you within the hour' — specific enough that they know I've actually looked at it and know roughly when to expect more, rather than a vague 'we're on it' that tells them nothing.
commonMistakes: Going silent until the root cause is fully found instead of sending a specific interim update
Guessing at the cause instead of checking refresh history and filters methodically
Sending a vague 'we're looking into it' instead of naming what's specifically being checked
Fixing the symptom without identifying why it happened, risking a repeat next refresh cycle
keyPoints: Investigation and communication should happen in parallel, not sequentially
A methodical check order: refresh history, source data presence, then report-level filters
A specific interim update is far more useful than a vague one or silence
The regional manager should know roughly when to expect a further update

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a methodical, logically ordered investigation
Describes a specific, honest interim communication, not silence or vagueness
Recognizes investigation and communication should happen together
Mentions follow-up to prevent recurrence
